site.name: Louisville Coal Mining Town & Hecla–Monarch Mine Landscape
site.location: Louisville / Hecla Mine / Northern Colorado Coalfield
site.category: Coal Mining Town / Mine / Railroad Landscape
overview: Louisville grew from the Northern Colorado coalfield after large coal deposits were developed in the late 1870s, and mining remained central to the town's economy and community for decades.

The Hecla Mine northeast of town became a major industrial and labor-history site, while Louisville miners also worked at nearby operations including the Monarch No. 2, whose 1936 explosion killed eight men and deeply affected the community.

timeline.text: Coal development accelerated on the Louisville townsite area, and Louisville emerged as a coal-mining community in the Northern Colorado coalfield.
The Hecla operation developed northeast of Louisville; historical accounts document two Hecla shafts and later consolidation of the mine.

The Hecla Mine became a center of the long Northern Coalfield strike. Armed guards, striking miners, and later federal troops made the Louisville area a significant northern episode of Colorado's coal-labor conflict.
An explosion at Monarch No. 2 south of Louisville killed eight miners. Many victims and workers were connected to Louisville families, making the disaster a major event in local memory.
The last coal mines operating around Louisville closed as the Northern Coalfield's remaining coal became increasingly uneconomic to mine.

moreHistory: Historic mapping identifies the Hecla Mine northeast of Louisville. Remnant uses the documented Hecla Mine locality near 39.99304, -105.12526 as the identification point for this broader Louisville coal-mining landscape; it is not presented as a field-surveyed surviving shaft or structure.

Louisville was unusual among some coal communities because the town itself was not a company-owned camp. Miners and their families built a community whose neighborhoods, businesses, immigrant traditions, rail connections, and labor history were closely tied to the mines.

The Monarch No. 2 mine was south of Louisville near today's Flatiron Crossing area, not at the Hecla identification point. Its 1936 explosion killed eight miners; two men escaped, and the disaster remained closely associated with Louisville because many local residents worked at the mine or knew the victims.
